items.stem: Whom does Antigone call outside the gates at the start of the play?
options: Her sister Ismene
Her brother Eteocles
The elders of Thebes
A palace guard

items.stem: What has Creon's edict ordered for Polyneices?
options: That no one may bury or mourn him
That he be buried beside his father
That his body be sent back to Argos
That his name be struck from the city records

items.stem: What penalty does the edict set for anyone who breaks it?
options: Death by stoning
Exile from Thebes
A heavy fine paid in silver
Loss of all family land

items.stem: Complete Antigone's line: “No man shall say that I _____ a brother.”
options: honoured
welcomed
praised
betrayed

items.stem: Who fled from Thebes in the night, according to Ismene?
options: The Argive army
The elders of the city
Creon's household guards
The priests of Zeus

items.stem: Why does Ismene refuse to help?
options: She is afraid to defy the ruler's power
She thinks Polyneices deserves no burial
She has promised to marry Creon's son
She plans to leave Thebes that night

items.stem: What does Antigone ask Ismene to do with the secret?
options: Proclaim it to all the town
Keep it close and tell no one
Tell only the elders of the city
Write it down for the priests

items.stem: Complete Ismene's warning: “If thou succeed; but thou art doomed to _____.”
options: triumph
prosper
endure
fail

items.stem: Who does Antigone say will be buried with full honours?
options: Eteocles
Polyneices
Menoeceus
Oedipus

items.stem: Which birds does Antigone say will feed on the unburied body?
options: Kites
Eagles
Owls
Swans

items.stem: Complete Antigone's line: “I will go alone To lap my dearest brother in the _____.”
options: palace
market
harbour
grave

items.stem: What does Ismene call the rule she would rather not overstep?
options: The golden mean
The law of the hearth
The will of the elders
The oath of the city

items.stem: What does Antigone mean when she says Ismene must show “If thou art worthy of thy blood or base”?
options: Ismene must prove her noble birth by acting
Ismene must prove she is truly Creon's niece
Ismene must swear an oath on her family's blood
Ismene must show she is braver than her brothers

items.stem: Why does Ismene speak of herself and Antigone as “weak women”?
options: She argues they cannot fight the stronger men who rule
She is mocking her sister for having so little courage to act
She is repeating an insult Creon has used
She wants the elders to take pity on them

items.stem: What does Antigone mean by calling herself “A sinless sinner”?
options: Breaking the edict would be right in the gods' eyes
She has done many wrongs that no one has seen
She expects the city to forgive her quickly
She is ashamed of what her brother did

items.stem: What is the effect of the quick one-line exchanges near the end of the scene?
options: They sharpen the clash between the sisters
They slow the scene into a calm prayer
They show that the sisters now agree
They let a third speaker join the debate

items.stem: Why does Antigone call the decree “aimed At thee and me”?
options: As sisters, they are the ones bound to bury him
Creon has named both sisters in a public speech
The guards have been told to watch their house
Creon believes they helped the Argive army

items.stem: What does Antigone's sarcasm in “our most noble Creon” suggest?
options: Contempt for the man who made the edict
Real respect for her uncle and for the way he governs
Fear that Creon will hear of her plan
Hope that Creon will change his mind

items.stem: Complete Antigone's question: “What right has he to keep me from my _____?”
options: foe
king
city
own

items.stem: What does Antigone's demand that Ismene proclaim her plan reveal?
options: She wants her act to be open and public
She hopes to be stopped before she acts
She does not trust the guards to report it
She wants Ismene to join her in the punishment

items.stem: Which device is at work in “Sister and brother linked in love’s embrace”?
options: Alliteration
Rhetorical question
Understatement
Apostrophe

items.stem: How does the Prologue shape the audience's expectations?
options: It sets a clear choice and a deadly penalty before Creon appears
It shows Creon explaining his edict to the city
It reveals at once how the conflict will end
It suggests that the sisters will soon agree

items.stem: Which pair of values does the Prologue set against each other?
options: Duty to family and the gods against obedience to the city
Love of wealth against love of honour
Courage in war against love of peace
Youth against the wisdom of old age

items.stem: What does Ismene mean by “Thou hast a fiery soul for numbing work”?
options: Antigone is passionate about a chilling, deadly task
Antigone is too cold to feel grief for her brother
Antigone works hard but has no real feeling
Antigone's anger will soon cool down

items.stem: Complete Antigone's reply: “When strength shall fail me, yes, but not _____.”
options: before
after
never
alone

items.stem: What is the effect of Antigone's word “disappointed” for Polyneices's lack of rites?
options: It stresses that he was denied what was owed him
It shows that he had fully expected to win the war and the throne
It suggests that the gods are angry with Creon
It means that Polyneices has been forgotten

items.stem: Why does Antigone add “if report speak true” when describing the edict?
options: She has heard it only by report so far
She believes the report is a lie
She wants to mock the city's heralds
She plans to ask Creon whether it is true

items.stem: How does Ismene's closing couplet (“Yet to thy lovers thou art dear as ever”) change the tone of the scene?
options: It ends the quarrel with loyal love
It turns the scene into open mockery
It warns that the gods will punish her
It shows that Ismene has changed her mind

items.stem: Which statement best describes the Prologue's role in the play?
options: It sets up the clash of city law and family duty
It explains in full how the war began
It shows the elders' first reactions to Creon
It gives the audience Creon's reasons for the edict
